title: Quantum jumps of sound
authors: Takuma Makihara, Erik Szakiel, Matthew P. Maksymowych, Oliver A. Hitchcock, Kaveh Pezeshki, Rachel G. Gruenke-Freudenstein, Mihir Pendharkar, Shannon P. Harvey, David I. Schuster, Amir H. Safavi-Naeini
abstract: Quantum mechanics predicts that a vibrating object's energy comes in discrete packets, yet no measurement of its position reveals this discreteness. Resolving individual energy levels requires a qualitatively different measurement, one coupling to the resonator's energy rather than its displacement. We use a superconducting qubit dispersively coupled to a nanomechanical resonator to perform repeated quantum nondemolition measurements of the phonon number. An aligned transfer-print technique integrating the qubit and resonator yields a mechanical lifetime of $T_1 = 2.1$ milliseconds and a dispersive shift of $2χ/2π= 328$ kilohertz per phonon. We heralded single-phonon states with 85% fidelity and observed quantum jumps between the resonator's first excited state and ground state. These discontinuous transitions are a striking manifestation of quantum mechanics in a massive, vibrating object.
summary: This experiment demonstrates the direct measurement of quantized mechanical energy in a nanomechanical resonator coupled to a superconducting qubit. By performing repeated quantum nondemolition measurements, the researchers observed clear quantum jumps between the ground and first excited states. This work marks a significant step in applying quantum control techniques to macroscopic mechanical systems.
main_problem: The goal was to observe the quantized nature of mechanical energy (phonon number discreteness) in a massive, vibrating object, which is otherwise hidden when measuring displacement.
main_result: The authors successfully observed quantum jumps between the resonator's first excited state and ground state, and heralded a single-phonon state with 85% fidelity.
method: They used repeated quantum nondemolition (QND) measurements of the phonon number, implemented by coupling a superconducting qubit to a nanomechanical resonator.
model_or_system: The system involves a nanomechanical resonator (e.g., in lithium niobate) dispersively coupled to a superconducting transmon qubit. The dynamics are governed by an effective Hamiltonian allowing QND measurement of the phonon number ($\hat{n}$).
key_observables: Phonon number distribution $P(n)$, quantum jumps between $|n=1angle$ and $|n=0angle$, and the mechanical lifetime ($T_1$).
important_parameters: Mechanical lifetime ($T_1 \approx 2.1$ ms or $645 \mu$s), dispersive shift ($2\chi/2\pi = 328$ kHz/phonon), and single-shot parity assignment fidelity (0.68 to 0.912).
main_assumptions: The measurement process is significantly faster than the phonon lifetime, and the forward-backward algorithm is used to estimate the true state evolution from noisy measurement records.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device architecture, postselected qubit spectra showing phonon number peaks, and individual measurement trajectories demonstrating abrupt quantum jumps between energy levels.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical need to measure energy directly, details the superconducting qubit/nanomechanical resonator platform, presents the QND measurement protocol using parity checks, and finally reports the observation of quantum jumps and state preparation fidelity.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, high-fidelity demonstration of quantum measurement backaction on a macroscopic mechanical oscillator, extending quantum control concepts from superconducting circuits and trapped ions to mechanical systems.

If an observer measures ⟨ˆx(t)⟩and calculates the energy of the resonator as ⟨ˆx(t)⟩2, a continu- ous exponential decay results. (B) If an observer can directly measure ˆx2(t) of a mechanical resonator, then quantum jumps in the mechanical energy can be observed. By using a qubit and mechanical resonator coupled in the dispersive regime, one can directly measure ˆx2(t). FIG. 2. Postselected qubit spectra. (A) Illustration of the qubit excitation spectrum in the strong dispersive regime. The area under the peak centered at zero frequency offset (2χ frequency offset) is proportional to the probability of measuring n = 0 (n = 1) phonons in the mechanical resonator. (B) Qubit spectrum measured with no parity checks, representing the initial coherent state of the mechanics. (C to H) Qubit spectrum postselected on k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 consecutive QND parity measurements, where every measurement outcome is |e⟩. As we observe more consecutive measurements of the qubit in the excited state, we become more certain that our mechanical resonator is in the n = 1 state,...

FIG. 3. Evolution of P(n=1) with postselection. The purple circles illustrate P(n = 1) from the postselected qubit spectra in Fig. 2. Consecutive measurement outcomes of |e⟩ increase P(n=1) through projection of the mechanical state, reflecting the information we learn after each measurement outcome. The gray shaded region illustrates a fit obtained through forward-propagating P(n) using Bayesian inference, where we fit P(e|even) and α of the initial coherent state. The error bars and shaded region represent 95% confidence intervals of the data and fit respectively.

FIG. 4. Quantum jumps of a mechanical resonator. Three individual measurement trajectories (rows), each consisting of 294 consecutive QND parity measurements on a mechanical resonator heralded in a single-phonon state with P(n = 1) = 0.85. (A, D, and G) Raw qubit measurement outcomes q ∈{g, e} after each Ramsey sequence. The dotted lines show the most- probable phonon number at each time step from forward-backward estimation. In each trajectory, an abrupt transition from predominantly |e⟩to predominantly |g⟩marks a quantum jump from n = 1 to n = 0.
